1.q: A 68-year-old woman with a mechanical mitral valve has a fever of 38.8 °C (101.8 °F), and two separate blood cultures grow Staphylococcus aureus. A transthoracic echocardiogram shows no vegetation. Which is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Transesophageal echocardiography

Correct. Transesophageal echocardiography is highly sensitive and specific, detects vegetations and defines the extent of disease, and it is required for optimal assessment of possible prosthetic valve endocarditis. A clear transthoracic study does not settle the question in a prosthetic valve with Staphylococcus aureus in the blood.
Treat for 1 week, then reassess

A week of treatment is far short of endocarditis therapy, typically 4-6 weeks from the first negative culture, and it skips the imaging she needs. The transesophageal study defines whether the prosthesis is infected.
right action at the wrong stage or severity
Stop the workup; echo was normal

Even a normal transesophageal echocardiogram does not necessarily rule out endocarditis, and hers was only transthoracic. With a typical organism in two cultures and a prosthetic valve, the transesophageal study comes next.
common lay belief
Repeat transthoracic study in 6 weeks

Waiting 6 weeks for another transthoracic study leaves a prosthetic valve infection unassessed. The transesophageal study is the one required for optimal assessment of possible prosthetic valve endocarditis.
right action at the wrong stage or severity

1.q: A 64-year-old man completed 4 weeks of ceftriaxone for Streptococcus gallolyticus (bovis) endocarditis. A colonoscopy last week was normal. Which other condition is this organism associated with?
opts: Urinary tract infection
The genitourinary tract is the source of enterococci. Streptococcus gallolyticus is linked to gastrointestinal abnormalities and to liver disease or cirrhosis.
adjacent fact from the same lecture
Dental infection
Dental infection and poor dentition are the source of viridans streptococci, the oral organisms. Streptococcus gallolyticus is a gastrointestinal organism linked to colon cancer and liver disease.

Liver disease or cirrhosis

Correct. Streptococcus gallolyticus (bovis) is associated with gastrointestinal abnormalities, especially colon cancer, and with liver disease or cirrhosis. With a normal colonoscopy, liver disease is the other association to keep in mind.
Injection drug use
Injection drug use is linked to Staphylococcus aureus, which causes most endocarditis in people who inject drugs. Streptococcus gallolyticus is associated with colon cancer and liver disease.

Oral amoxicillin, recheck in 1 week

Outpatient echo next week, no labs

1.q: Four patients are on day 5 of appropriate intravenous antibiotics for native valve endocarditis. Which one needs evaluation for surgery?
opts: Fever resolved, cultures now negative
A settled fever and negative cultures mean the infection is responding; that is the opposite of the 'not resolving with appropriate antibiotics' indication. This patient continues the course.
reversed direction or value
Mild anemia with a normal cell size

A normocytic anemia of chronic disease is an expected lab finding in endocarditis, not a surgical indication. Surgery is for heart failure from valve dysfunction, persistent infection, abscess or fungal infection.
adjacent fact from the same lecture
New heart failure from severe regurgitation

Correct. Heart failure due to valvular dysfunction is the most common indication for surgery, alongside infection not resolving on appropriate antibiotics, abscess and fungal infection. New heart failure from severe regurgitation calls for cardiothoracic surgery evaluation.
Splinter hemorrhages still visible
Splinter hemorrhages are a peripheral embolic sign and are not an indication for surgery. Heart failure from valvular dysfunction is the most common indication.

1.q: A patient with which of the following conditions requires antimicrobial prophylaxis before dental surgery?
opts: Atrial septal defect

An atrial septal defect is not one of the high-risk conditions; only unrepaired cyanotic congenital heart disease or repaired disease with a residual defect at a prosthetic patch or device qualifies. An isolated atrial septal defect is even excluded from the Duke predisposing conditions.
adjacent fact from the same lecture
Previous coronary artery bypass grafting

Coronary bypass surgery does not place prosthetic valve material and is not a high-risk condition, so it does not call for endocarditis prophylaxis. The list covers prosthetic valves or repair material, previous endocarditis, certain congenital heart disease and transplant valvulopathy.
common lay belief
Mitral valve prolapse, no regurgitation

Mitral valve prolapse without regurgitation is not on the high-risk list. Prophylaxis before dental work is for prosthetic valves or repair material, previous endocarditis, certain congenital heart disease and cardiac transplant with valve regurgitation.
common lay belief
Previous infective endocarditis

Correct. Prophylaxis is reserved for high-risk cardiac conditions: prosthetic valves or valve-repair material, previous infective endocarditis, certain congenital heart disease and cardiac transplant with valve regurgitation. A past episode of endocarditis is on that list, so dental work that manipulates the gums or tooth roots needs prophylaxis.

1.q: A 28-year-old man with a history of injection drug use is evaluated in the emergency department for fever and fatigue. He is cachectic and diaphoretic. His pulse is regular at 110 beats per minute, temperature 38.4 °C (101.1 °F) orally and blood pressure 128/68 mm Hg (right arm, seated). A high-pitched murmur is heard along the left lower sternal border, and small painless hemorrhages are noted on the conjunctivae, palate and palms. What is the recommended initial treatment?
opts: Intramuscular penicillin, one dose

A single intramuscular dose is a prophylaxis-style regimen, not treatment. Endocarditis therapy must be bactericidal, parenteral (intravenous) and prolonged, typically 4-6 weeks from the first negative blood culture, and penicillin would not cover methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus.
confused mechanism or drug class
Follow lactic acid, start antibiotics if above 2.5 mmol/L

Waiting for a lab threshold delays treatment of a febrile, tachycardic patient whose findings already suggest endocarditis. When the picture suggests acute endocarditis, two blood cultures are drawn within the first 1-2 hours and empiric antibiotics follow; no lactic acid level is needed to start them.
right action at the wrong stage or severity
Begin an aminoglycoside with penicillin and cefepime

This mixes pieces of other regimens. The three-drug empiric regimen with an aminoglycoside (gentamicin) and cefepime is for a prosthetic valve placed within the last year, and it is built on vancomycin, not penicillin. He has a native valve, and methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus needs vancomycin or daptomycin.
right action at the wrong stage or severity
Begin vancomycin, adjust per blood culture results

Correct. Fever, tachycardia, a new left lower sternal border murmur and painless hemorrhages on the conjunctivae, palate and palms in a person who injects drugs point to endocarditis, most often from Staphylococcus aureus, which may be methicillin-resistant. Vancomycin begins once blood cultures are drawn and is adjusted when the organism and its sensitivities return.

1.q: A 69-year-old man with a bioprosthetic aortic valve is scheduled for bronchoscopy, during which a biopsy of the airway mucosa is planned. He has no drug allergies and takes pills. Which plan fits?
opts: No prophylaxis for bronchoscopy

Bronchoscopy is exempt only when it involves no incision of the mucosa. A planned biopsy of the airway mucosa makes it an invasive respiratory procedure, which in a high-risk patient needs prophylaxis.
ruled out by a stated finding
Oral amoxicillin beforehand

Correct. A prosthetic valve is high risk, and invasive respiratory procedures that incise or biopsy the respiratory mucosa call for prophylaxis. Bronchoscopy is exempt only when no mucosal incision such as a biopsy is made; his includes one, so he takes a single oral amoxicillin dose 30-60 minutes before.
Oral clindamycin beforehand
Clindamycin is no longer recommended for prophylaxis because of the risk of Clostridioides difficile infection, and he has no penicillin allergy. Oral amoxicillin is the standard agent.
adjacent fact from the same lecture
Amoxicillin for 3 days after
Prophylaxis is a single dose 30-60 minutes BEFORE the procedure, not a course afterward; the drug must be circulating when the biopsy lets bacteria into the blood.
reversed direction or value

1.q: A 74-year-old man was recently diagnosed with colon adenocarcinoma. He now has 3 weeks of low-grade fever and a new murmur, and transesophageal echocardiography shows a mitral valve vegetation. He has had no dental work, urinary symptoms or drug use. Which organism is most likely?
opts: Enterococcus faecalis
Enterococci come from the genitourinary tract, and he has no urinary symptoms. The organism linked to colon cancer is Streptococcus gallolyticus.

Streptococcus gallolyticus

Correct. Streptococcus gallolyticus (bovis) comes from the gastrointestinal tract and is associated with gastrointestinal abnormalities, especially colon cancer, and with liver disease. His new colon cancer, with no dental, urinary or injection source, points to it.
Viridans streptococci

competing diagnosis
Staphylococcus aureus
Staphylococci come from the skin, and Staphylococcus aureus dominates in people who inject drugs. He has no drug use; his colon cancer points to Streptococcus gallolyticus.

1.q: A 46-year-old woman with rheumatic mitral regurgitation has 6 weeks of low-grade fever, night sweats and weight loss. Transesophageal echocardiography shows a mitral vegetation, and three sets of blood cultures grow Aggregatibacter actinomycetemcomitans, a HACEK (Haemophilus, Aggregatibacter, Cardiobacterium, Eikenella, Kingella) organism. She had anaphylaxis to penicillin. Which antibiotic class could be considered?
opts: Ampicillin-sulbactam
Ampicillin-sulbactam is a listed HACEK regimen, but ampicillin is a penicillin and she had anaphylaxis to penicillin. With that allergy a fluoroquinolone is the class to consider instead.
ruled out by a stated finding
Vancomycin plus gentamicin

Vancomycin plus gentamicin is an enterococcal regimen and is not listed for HACEK organisms, which are gram-negative. For HACEK endocarditis in a patient allergic to penicillin, a fluoroquinolone could be considered.
adjacent fact from the same lecture
A fluoroquinolone

Correct. HACEK (Haemophilus, Aggregatibacter, Cardiobacterium, Eikenella, Kingella) endocarditis is treated with ceftriaxone or another third-generation cephalosporin, and for a patient with a penicillin allergy a fluoroquinolone could be considered. Her anaphylaxis to penicillin is the comorbidity that points to this class.
Nafcillin or oxacillin

Nafcillin and oxacillin are penicillins used for methicillin-susceptible Staphylococcus aureus. Her organism is a gram-negative HACEK organism, and her anaphylaxis to penicillin rules these out twice over; a fluoroquinolone could be considered.

opts: Intravenous ceftriaxone

Correct. A prosthetic valve is a high-risk condition, and an extraction manipulates the gums. A patient with no penicillin allergy who cannot take oral medication gets an injection: ampicillin, or cefazolin or ceftriaxone, intramuscular or intravenous, 30-60 minutes before the procedure.
Oral amoxicillin

Oral amoxicillin is the standard regimen, but she is intubated and cannot take anything by mouth. The regimen for a patient unable to take oral medication is ampicillin, cefazolin or ceftriaxone by injection.

Intravenous clindamycin
Clindamycin is no longer recommended for endocarditis prophylaxis because of the risk of Clostridioides difficile infection, by any route. Ampicillin, cefazolin or ceftriaxone by injection fits her.

Oral azithromycin
Azithromycin is an oral option for penicillin-ALLERGIC patients. She has no allergy and cannot swallow, so she needs an injectable agent such as ceftriaxone.

1.q: An 80-year-old woman had her mitral valve replaced with a bioprosthesis 3 years ago. She now has 2 weeks of fever to 38.9 °C (102.0 °F), fatigue and a new regurgitant murmur. Three sets of blood cultures have been drawn, and results are pending. Which empiric regimen is most appropriate?
opts: Vancomycin, gentamicin and cefepime

The three-drug regimen of vancomycin, gentamicin and cefepime is for a prosthetic valve in place 1 year or LESS. Her valve was placed 3 years ago, so she gets the regimen used for older prostheses, vancomycin plus ceftriaxone.
right action at the wrong stage or severity
Vancomycin plus ceftriaxone

Correct. Empiric therapy covers staphylococci, streptococci and enterococci. Vancomycin plus ceftriaxone is the regimen for native valve endocarditis, a subacute presentation, or a prosthetic valve in place MORE than 1 year, and her bioprosthesis is 3 years old.
Ceftriaxone alone

Ceftriaxone alone leaves staphylococci, including methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus, uncovered. Empiric therapy must cover staphylococci, streptococci and enterococci, so ceftriaxone is paired with vancomycin.

Nafcillin plus gentamicin

Nafcillin is a directed drug for methicillin-susceptible Staphylococcus aureus, not empiric therapy. Before the organism is known, the regimen must cover methicillin-resistant staphylococci too, which is why vancomycin anchors every empiric regimen.

1.q: A 73-year-old man with a mechanical aortic valve placed 6 years ago has Staphylococcus aureus endocarditis of the prosthesis and was started on vancomycin, rifampin and gentamicin. Susceptibility testing now shows methicillin-susceptible Staphylococcus aureus, and he has no drug allergies. Which change is appropriate?
opts: Stop rifampin and gentamicin

Dropping rifampin and gentamicin would leave a native-valve regimen. For Staphylococcus aureus on a prosthetic valve both stay in the combination; the change a methicillin-susceptible result allows is nafcillin or oxacillin in place of vancomycin.
adjacent fact from the same lecture
Replace vancomycin with daptomycin

Daptomycin is the alternative to vancomycin for methicillin-RESISTANT Staphylococcus aureus. His isolate is methicillin-susceptible, so the swap is to nafcillin or oxacillin, the drugs for susceptible strains.
reversed direction or value
Switch to oral rifampin alone

Rifampin is one part of the prosthetic valve combination and is never used alone here; endocarditis therapy is parenteral, bactericidal and prolonged. He keeps rifampin and gentamicin, with nafcillin or oxacillin replacing vancomycin.
confused mechanism or drug class
Replace vancomycin with nafcillin

Correct. Staphylococcus aureus on a prosthetic valve is treated with an antistaphylococcal drug plus rifampin plus gentamicin. Vancomycin is the drug for methicillin-resistant strains; when cultures show a methicillin-susceptible strain, vancomycin can be changed to nafcillin or oxacillin while rifampin and gentamicin continue.

This reverses the fact: peripheral stigmata are considerably LESS common in children than in adults. Children with congenital heart disease more often have an indolent course of low-grade fever, fatigue and joint aches without the classic skin and eye signs.

They appear only with Candida
Peripheral signs are not specific to fungal infection; they appear with bacterial endocarditis in adults. In children they are simply less common.

Those signs are less common in children

Correct. Classic peripheral stigmata (Osler nodes, Janeway lesions, Roth spots, splinter hemorrhages) are considerably less common in children than in adults. A child with congenital heart disease usually has an indolent course, prolonged low-grade fever with fatigue and joint aches, as she does.

Missing peripheral signs do not rule out endocarditis, especially in a child, in whom they are considerably less common. Her positive viridans streptococcal cultures and history fit the disease.

Switch to ceftriaxone alone

Correct. Enterococcal endocarditis is treated with penicillin or ampicillin plus gentamicin, or with ampicillin plus ceftriaxone, and ampicillin plus ceftriaxone is the combination marked as good for chronic kidney disease or acute kidney injury with a low creatinine clearance. Nafcillin or oxacillin

Nafcillin or oxacillin treats methicillin-susceptible Staphylococcus aureus, not enterococci. His cultures grew Enterococcus faecalis, whose regimens are built on ampicillin (or penicillin), here paired with ceftriaxone because of his kidney disease.

Ampicillin plus gentamicin

Ampicillin plus gentamicin is a standard enterococcal regimen when kidney function is normal, but his creatinine clearance is 25 mL/min. The gentamicin-free alternative, ampicillin plus ceftriaxone, is the one listed for kidney disease with a low clearance.

2.q: A 52-year-old woman with previous infective endocarditis has four procedures planned this year. Before which one should she receive prophylaxis?
opts: Dental cleaning

Correct. Previous endocarditis makes her high risk, and prophylaxis is given for dental procedures that manipulate the gums or tooth roots, which includes dental cleaning. The other procedures are on the no-prophylaxis list.
Dental radiographs
Taking dental radiographs does not manipulate the gums or tooth roots and is listed as NOT needing prophylaxis, even in a high-risk patient. The cleaning is the procedure that does.
common lay belief
Screening colonoscopy

Gastrointestinal procedures such as colonoscopy do not need endocarditis prophylaxis in the absence of active infection. Prophylaxis is for dental work on the gums or roots and for invasive respiratory procedures.
common lay belief
Cystoscopy
Genitourinary procedures such as cystoscopy do not require endocarditis prophylaxis. In a high-risk patient, prophylaxis is given before dental work that manipulates the gums, such as a cleaning.

2.q: A 24-year-old man who uses intravenous drugs is admitted with 4 weeks of fever. An earlier echocardiogram showed a large aortic valve vegetation. Three blood cultures have grown Candida species, he is receiving fluconazole, and he suddenly develops a cold, blue toe. Which is the appropriate next step?
opts: Surgery consult for aortic valve replacement

Correct. Candida in three blood cultures with a large aortic vegetation is fungal endocarditis, and fungal infection is difficult to cure with medication alone, which makes it an indication for surgery. The cold, blue toe is the expected complication, embolism and occlusion of a larger peripheral artery, so the definitive step is cardiovascular surgery to replace the valve.
Switch fluconazole to amphotericin B

Changing the antifungal does not solve the problem: fungal endocarditis is difficult to cure with medication alone, which is why fungal infection is itself an indication for surgery. Source control by valve replacement, not a different drug, is the definitive management.
right action at the wrong stage or severity
Repeat echo to see if the vegetation embolized

The cold, blue toe already shows that the vegetation has embolized: embolism and occlusion of larger peripheral arteries is the most likely complication of fungal endocarditis. Another scan would not change the plan, which is surgery for a fungal infection that medication alone rarely cures.
right action at the wrong stage or severity
Aortic angiography for a mycotic aneurysm

A mycotic (infected) aneurysm is a recognized complication, but a cold toe with Candida in the blood and a large aortic vegetation is the expected embolic event of fungal endocarditis. Imaging the aorta delays the step that treats the source, valve surgery.
competing diagnosis

2.q: A 67-year-old man with a transcatheter aortic valve needs a tooth extraction. His chart lists a penicillin allergy: years ago he had a mild, delayed rash with penicillin, with no hives, swelling or breathing trouble. He takes pills. Which agent fits?
opts: Oral amoxicillin

Amoxicillin is the standard agent for patients WITHOUT a penicillin allergy. He reports an allergy (a rash), so he moves to the penicillin-allergy row: cephalexin, azithromycin or clarithromycin, or doxycycline.
ruled out by a stated finding
Oral cephalexin

Correct. A transcatheter-implanted prosthesis is a high-risk condition, and an extraction manipulates the gums. For a penicillin-allergic patient who can take pills, cephalexin is listed, and it is barred only after anaphylaxis, angioedema or urticaria, none of which he had.
Oral clindamycin
Clindamycin is no longer recommended for endocarditis prophylaxis because of the risk of Clostridioides difficile infection. With a mild rash only, cephalexin is an acceptable oral choice.
adjacent fact from the same lecture
Intravenous vancomycin
Vancomycin is not part of the adult prophylaxis regimens, and he can take pills. The oral penicillin-allergy options are cephalexin, azithromycin or clarithromycin, and doxycycline.

2.q: A 10-year-old girl had an atrial septal defect closed with a prosthetic device 3 years ago, and echocardiography shows no residual shunt. She needs a dental extraction. Which is appropriate regarding endocarditis prophylaxis?
opts: Prophylaxis only with a murmur

A murmur is not what decides prophylaxis. The pediatric list turns on prosthetic material, previous endocarditis, unrepaired cyanotic disease, the first 6 months after repair, or a residual defect next to the repair.
common lay belief
Give prophylaxis beforehand
She would qualify within the first 6 months after a device repair, or with a residual defect next to the device. Three years out with no residual shunt, she is not on the high-risk list.
right action at the wrong stage or severity
No prophylaxis is needed

Correct. Repaired congenital heart disease calls for prophylaxis only in the first 6 months after repair with prosthetic material or a device, or when a residual defect sits next to the prosthetic material. She is 3 years out with no residual shunt, so neither applies.
A 3-day course afterward
Prophylaxis, when indicated, is a single dose before the procedure, never a course afterward; and she does not need it at all, being 3 years past the repair with no residual shunt.

opts: Coronary stents and prior bypass
Coronary stents and bypass grafting place no valve material and are not high-risk conditions, so they do not call for endocarditis prophylaxis before dental work.
common lay belief
Mitral prolapse without regurgitation
Mitral valve prolapse without regurgitation is not on the high-risk list. Of these patients, only the transplant recipient with regurgitation from a structurally abnormal valve qualifies.
common lay belief
Heart transplant with valve regurgitation

Correct. Cardiac transplant with valve regurgitation from a structurally abnormal valve is on the high-risk list, together with prosthetic valves or repair material, previous endocarditis and certain congenital heart disease. An extraction manipulates the gums, so this patient needs prophylaxis.
Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy

Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is a predisposing condition in the Duke criteria, but it is not on the prophylaxis list. Prophylaxis is reserved for prosthetic valves or repair material, previous endocarditis, certain congenital heart disease and transplant valvulopathy.

2.q: A 64-year-old woman whose mitral valve was repaired with an annuloplasty ring needs a root canal. Years ago she developed lip and tongue swelling (angioedema) after ampicillin. She takes pills easily. Which prophylaxis fits?
opts: Intramuscular cefazolin
Cefazolin by injection is for penicillin-allergic patients who CANNOT take oral medication, and it is a cephalosporin, barred by her angioedema. She swallows pills, so oral clarithromycin fits.
ruled out by a stated finding
Oral clarithromycin

Correct. Prosthetic material used for valve repair, such as an annuloplasty ring, is a high-risk condition, and a root canal manipulates the periapical region, so she needs prophylaxis. With a penicillin allergy and an oral route, clarithromycin or azithromycin (or doxycycline) fits; her angioedema bars cephalosporins.
No prophylaxis needed
She does need it: prosthetic material used for cardiac valve repair (annuloplasty rings, chords or clips) is on the high-risk list, and a root canal manipulates the periapical region of the tooth.
ruled out by a stated finding
Oral cephalexin

Cephalexin is an oral option for penicillin allergy, but cephalosporins should not be used after anaphylaxis, angioedema or urticaria to penicillin or ampicillin. Her lip and tongue swelling was angioedema, so a macrolide such as clarithromycin is used.

2.q: A 69-year-old woman had her aortic valve replaced with a prosthesis 3 months ago. She asks when her risk of prosthetic valve endocarditis is highest. Which answer is accurate?
opts: Within the first year

Correct. The greatest risk of prosthetic valve endocarditis is within the first year after replacement; it then gradually declines until it is similar to the risk for a native valve. At 3 months she is inside that window.
From year 2 to year 5
The risk is highest earlier, within the first year after replacement, and it declines afterward rather than peaking in years 2 to 5.
reversed direction or value
After 10 years

Risk does not climb late. It is greatest within the first year after replacement and then gradually falls until it is similar to native-valve risk, so a valve 10 years old carries less risk than hers does now.
reversed direction or value
The same at all times
The risk is not constant: it is greatest within the first year after replacement and then gradually declines until it matches native valve risk.

2.q: A 71-year-old man with type 2 diabetes is on day 3 of ampicillin plus gentamicin for Enterococcus faecalis endocarditis of his native aortic valve. His creatinine has risen from 1.0 to 2.6 mg/dL (normal 0.6-1.2), an acute kidney injury, and his creatinine clearance has fallen. Which change is most appropriate?
opts: Replace gentamicin with ceftriaxone

Correct. Ampicillin plus ceftriaxone is the enterococcal combination marked as good for acute kidney injury or chronic kidney disease with a low creatinine clearance. Swapping gentamicin for ceftriaxone keeps a bactericidal two-drug regimen against the enterococcus while removing the drug kept away from failing kidneys.
Continue ampicillin plus gentamicin

Ampicillin plus gentamicin suits normal kidney function, but his creatinine has more than doubled. The listed alternative for acute kidney injury with a low creatinine clearance is ampicillin plus ceftriaxone, so the regimen should change rather than continue.
ruled out by a stated finding
Switch to oral amoxicillin

Endocarditis antibiotics are given parenterally (intravenously) and for weeks, so a switch to pills on day 3 is not an option. The fix for his kidney injury is to drop gentamicin and pair ampicillin with ceftriaxone.
confused mechanism or drug class
Stop antibiotics until it recovers

Pausing treatment leaves bacteria alive in the vegetation, and every one of them must be killed with bactericidal therapy, typically 4-6 weeks from the first negative culture. The kidney injury calls for a different partner drug, not a pause.

2.q: A 29-year-old woman who injects drugs has a temperature of 39.0 °C (102.2 °F) and a cough, and chest imaging shows septic pulmonary infarcts. One of three blood cultures grows Staphylococcus aureus. Transthoracic and transesophageal echocardiography show no vegetation, abscess or new regurgitation. What is her modified Duke classification?
opts: Possible: four minor criteria

Correct. Injection drug use, fever, septic pulmonary infarcts (a vascular phenomenon) and a single positive culture that does not meet the major criterion are four minor criteria, with no major one. Three or more minor criteria make the case possible; definite needs five.
Definite: one major, three minor
One positive culture of three is not the major criterion, which needs a typical organism in two separate cultures, and the echocardiograms show no endocardial involvement. She has no major criterion.
confused mechanism or drug class
Definite: five minor criteria
She has four minor criteria, not five: injection drug use, fever, septic pulmonary infarcts and the single positive culture. There is no immunologic finding to make a fifth.
confused mechanism or drug class
Ruled out by the normal echo
A normal transesophageal echocardiogram does not necessarily rule out endocarditis. Her four minor criteria still make it possible.
common lay belief

2.q: A 66-year-old woman with a mechanical aortic valve is being evaluated for endocarditis. She has a fever of 38.9 °C (102.0 °F), and blood cultures are pending. Which finding would count as a major modified Duke criterion?
opts: Painful red nodules on finger pads

Painful finger-pad nodules (Osler nodes) are an immunologic phenomenon, a MINOR criterion. Major criteria are a typical positive blood culture and echocardiographic evidence such as new partial dehiscence.
confused mechanism or drug class
Pinpoint conjunctival hemorrhages
Conjunctival hemorrhages are a vascular phenomenon, a MINOR criterion. New partial dehiscence of her prosthetic valve would be a major one.
confused mechanism or drug class
Her prosthetic valve itself
Having a prosthetic valve is a predisposing heart condition, a MINOR criterion. A major criterion would be echocardiographic evidence such as new partial dehiscence of that valve.
confused mechanism or drug class
New partial dehiscence of the valve

Correct. Evidence of endocardial involvement is a major criterion, and new partial dehiscence of a prosthetic valve on echocardiography is one of its forms, along with an oscillating intracardiac mass and an abscess. The other findings are minor criteria.

One of three blood cultures grows viridans streptococci, and transesophageal echocardiography shows a vegetation on the mitral valve. What is her modified Duke classification?
opts: Possible: one major, one minor
She has more than one minor criterion: fever, conjunctival hemorrhages and the single positive culture. With the vegetation that is one major plus three minor, definite.
confused mechanism or drug class
Definite: two major criteria

The blood-culture major criterion needs a typical organism in TWO separate cultures; she has one of three. That single culture counts as a minor criterion, so she is definite by one major plus three minor.
confused mechanism or drug class
Definite: one major, three minor

Correct. The mitral vegetation is a major criterion. Fever, conjunctival hemorrhages (vascular) and a single positive culture that does not meet the major criterion (microbiologic) are three minor criteria. One major plus three minor is definite.

2.q: A 62-year-old woman has native aortic valve endocarditis from viridans streptococci after a dental extraction. She had anaphylaxis to penicillin, and hives after ceftriaxone. Which antibiotic fits?
opts: Ceftriaxone plus gentamicin
Ceftriaxone plus gentamicin is a viridans streptococcal regimen, but she had hives after ceftriaxone. With reactions to both penicillin and ceftriaxone, vancomycin is the option left.
ruled out by a stated finding
Penicillin G
Penicillin G is a first choice for viridans streptococci, but she had anaphylaxis to penicillin, which rules it out. Vancomycin is the listed streptococcal option that avoids both of her allergies.
ruled out by a stated finding
Nafcillin
Nafcillin is a penicillin used for methicillin-susceptible Staphylococcus aureus. Her organism is a viridans streptococcus and she is allergic to penicillin, so vancomycin fits.
confused mechanism or drug class
Vancomycin

Correct. Viridans streptococci are treated with penicillin G or ceftriaxone (with or without gentamicin) or with vancomycin. Her anaphylaxis to penicillin and her hives after ceftriaxone rule out the first two, leaving vancomycin as the listed alternative.

2.q: A 68-year-old man is hospitalized with Streptococcus bovis (gallolyticus) endocarditis of the mitral valve. He recovers completely with appropriate therapy. Which is the most important next step?
opts: Repeat echocardiography in 6 weeks

He recovered completely, and nothing in his course calls for a follow-up scan of the valve. What his organism does call for is a search of the colon: Streptococcus gallolyticus is linked to gastrointestinal abnormalities, especially colon cancer.
right action at the wrong stage or severity
Mitral valve replacement to prevent emboli

Surgery is for heart failure from valve dysfunction, infection not resolving on appropriate antibiotics, an abscess or a fungal infection. He has none of these and recovered completely; the next step is a colonoscopy because of the organism's link to colon cancer.
right action at the wrong stage or severity
Dental hygiene and denture fitting

Oral hygiene targets the mouth's flora, viridans streptococci, the classic organism after dental work. His organism is Streptococcus gallolyticus, a gastrointestinal organism, so the source to look for is in the colon, not the teeth.
adjacent fact from the same lecture
Colonoscopy to look for mucosal lesions

Correct. Streptococcus gallolyticus (bovis) comes from the gastrointestinal tract and is associated with liver disease or cirrhosis and with gastrointestinal abnormalities, especially colon cancer. Once the endocarditis is cured, the most important step is looking for the colonic lesion that let the organism into the blood.

2.q: A 59-year-old man with a bioprosthetic aortic valve placed 6 years ago has subacute endocarditis, and three sets of blood cultures grow Cardiobacterium hominis. He had hives and throat swelling after amoxicillin, and hives again after a dose of ceftriaxone last year. Which antibiotic fits?

Nafcillin or oxacillin

confused mechanism or drug class
Ceftriaxone

ruled out by a stated finding
A fluoroquinolone

Correct. Cardiobacterium hominis is a HACEK (Haemophilus, Aggregatibacter, Cardiobacterium, Eikenella, Kingella) organism, normally treated with ceftriaxone or another third-generation cephalosporin. He has reacted to both a penicillin and ceftriaxone, and for HACEK disease with a penicillin allergy a fluoroquinolone could be considered.

2.q: A 48-year-old woman with normal kidney function has uncomplicated native mitral valve endocarditis from penicillin-susceptible viridans streptococci. Her fever settled within 2 days of starting therapy, and she has no abscess or heart failure. The team wants the shortest course a regimen allows. Which regimen fits?
opts: Ampicillin plus ceftriaxone

Ampicillin plus ceftriaxone is an enterococcal regimen, given for 6 weeks. Her organism is a viridans streptococcus, not an enterococcus, so the regimen that offers the shortest course is ceftriaxone plus gentamicin for 2 weeks.
adjacent fact from the same lecture
Vancomycin alone
Vancomycin is a listed alternative for viridans streptococci, but it is given for 4 weeks and has no short-course version. The 2-week option is penicillin G or ceftriaxone plus gentamicin.
adjacent fact from the same lecture
Ceftriaxone alone

Ceftriaxone alone is a correct drug for susceptible viridans streptococci, but without gentamicin it runs the full 4 weeks. Only the combination with gentamicin qualifies for the 2-week course in uncomplicated, rapidly responding disease.
right action at the wrong stage or severity
Ceftriaxone plus gentamicin

Correct. Adding gentamicin to penicillin G or ceftriaxone allows a 2-week regimen for viridans streptococcal endocarditis, but only when it is uncomplicated, responds rapidly and there is no chronic kidney disease. She meets all three, so the combination gives the shortest course.

Gastrointestinal tract

Upper respiratory tract

Skin surface

2.q: A 5-year-old boy with congenital heart disease has infective endocarditis. His parents ask how children's endocarditis differs from adults'. Compared with adults, which feature is more typical in children?
opts: Mostly degenerative valve disease

Pediatric endocarditis is driven overwhelmingly by congenital heart disease and indwelling central venous catheters rather than degenerative valve disease. What is more typical in children is right-sided disease.
adjacent fact from the same lecture
More peripheral skin signs

Classic peripheral stigmata such as Osler nodes, Janeway lesions and Roth spots are considerably less common in children than in adults, so their absence in a child proves little. Right-sided disease is what is more common in children.
reversed direction or value
More often right-sided

Correct. Compared with adults, pediatric endocarditis is more often right-sided, particularly with congenital heart disease, carries a higher septic embolism rate and causes less heart failure. Peripheral stigmata are less common.
More heart failure
Children with endocarditis have LESS heart failure than adults; the risk rises only in those without congenital heart disease, whose disease mirrors adults'.
reversed direction or value
